In order to have a sympathetic villain, you have to be able to comprehend their motives, which is not inherently a good thing, if your goal is to foster fear, awe, and a real sense of danger to the reader/viewer/whatever.

A villain you cannot comprehend is one you cannot predict, cannot reason or bargain with. The stakes are higher, because there will be no mercy. You have to win. The Reapers from Mass Effect were a great example of this, until they ruined them in ME3 by making them comprehensible, no matter how flawed the logic was.

That said, an incomprehensible villain is also a two dimensional one, often with limited back story. They are easy to hate, but that is about it. Being able to empathise with a villain and see them as a person with thoughts, feelings and ideas can increase the emotional impact of having to put an end to them later on in the story.

The God Generals from Tales of the Abyss are a nice example; usually I feel nothing when ploughing through the underlings on my way to the final boss, but killing some of those made me feel very bitter and forlorn, which I loved.

In short, it depends on what story you are trying to convey and what emotions you want to draw out from your reader/viewer/player etc...

There are other ways to inspire fear, but it's hard to get it right.

I always thought Zaheer from LoK was a decent example. On the one hand, he's a sympathetic villain... His motives are comprehensible, in fact he's quite articulate and expresses them well. He's not particularly powerful, as the Avatar (the protagonist of the series) is basically a god-on-earth. On the other hand, he is mad, easy to hate by the end, and worms his way into Korra's psyche. Hell, he does a ton of damage AFTER he is defeated.

Kreia is another extreme example.

I like both, but probably lean on the direction of the sympathetic villain. I like how the two sides play off one another and those moments between feeling sorry for the villain and wanting the villain to die by fire.

My absolute favorite villains are the grey villains who make you really think about their motives.

Revan is a good example, if you ever played KOTOR. He was undoubtedly evil, WAY past the point of being a "sympathetic" one... But at the same time, he was trying to save the Galaxy from something worse.

Come to think of it, KOTOR II in particular has ALOT of greyness for a universe that's notorious for sticking to black/white morals and redeemable/unredeemable villains. It's like they were trying to screw with Star Wars lore, and stretch the story patterns to a breaking point.

I definitely prefer using sympathetic villains in my own campaigns. As far as from a perspective of a DM in D&D, pure evil maniacal villains are easy to predict, doing evil for evils sake. They are more a force of nature than a thinking being most of the time. Sometimes all you want in your game is a pure good versus evil story, but the stories that stick with you almost always have a sympathetic villain at the top.

My all time favorite is Jon Irenicus from the Baldur's Gate series. From your original perception he seems to be evil for evils sake and evolves into a sympathetic villain as time goes on. Still undoubtedly evil, but you can see the path that led him to where he was and can see his walking the steady staircase into the abyss of evil.
Sometimes, shitty movies try to make unredeemably evil antagonists that I then relate to and root for for the duration of the film.

Does it take longer to render/process or something?
Is there a reason x265 is taking sooo long to catch on?

Hardware.

Older phones, tablets, desktops, laptops, streaming boxes, and cable boxes don't have a hardware decoding block for x265 video. That means it takes a ton of power (or battery) to play x265 on a larger computer (assuming the CPU can handle it), and it simply won't work on a lot of phones/tablets.

Software is another problem. People have a habit of using old video players with no x265 support, as the best, most modern players (Kodi/MPV on Linux, anything with LAV/MadVR on Windows) aren't particularly popular.
